questionText: Choose the correctly formed sentence:
options: A) Neither the manager nor the staff was satisfied.
B) Neither the manager nor the staff were satisfied.
C) Neither the manager nor the staff are satisfied.
D) Neither the manager nor staff was satisfied.
explanation: With NEITHER...NOR, the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. STAFF (singular collective noun) takes WAS.

questionText: Which sentence uses the subjunctive mood correctly?
options: A) If I was you, I would leave.
B) If I were you, I would leave.
C) If I am you, I would leave.
D) If I be you, I will leave.
explanation: The SUBJUNCTIVE mood uses WERE (not WAS) for hypothetical or contrary-to-fact conditions: If I WERE you... This applies regardless of singular or plural subject.

questionText: Complete the sentence: 'Had she studied harder, she ___ passed.'
options: A) would have
B) will have
C) would
D) had
explanation: This is a THIRD CONDITIONAL sentence — a past hypothetical. Structure: Had + past participle → WOULD HAVE + past participle.

questionText: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: A) The committee have made their decision.
B) The committee has made its decision.
C) The committee are made their decision.
D) The committee made their decisions.
explanation: In formal/American English, COMMITTEE is singular and takes HAS and ITS. British English sometimes treats collective nouns as plural.

questionText: Identify the sentence with correct parallel structure:
options: A) She likes reading, to swim, and hiking.
B) She likes reading, swimming, and to hike.
C) She likes reading, swimming, and hiking.
D) She likes to read, swimming, and hiking.
explanation: PARALLEL STRUCTURE requires all items in a list to use the same grammatical form. Reading, swimming, and hiking are all gerunds.

questionText: Choose the correct sentence:
options: A) Between you and I, this is a secret.
B) Between you and me, this is a secret.
C) Between I and you, this is a secret.
D) Between me and I, this is a secret.
explanation: Prepositions take OBJECT pronouns. BETWEEN is a preposition, so it must be followed by BETWEEN YOU AND ME, not I.

questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a restrictive clause?
options: A) The student, who won the prize, is my friend.
B) The student who won the prize is my friend.
C) The student which won the prize is my friend.
D) The student, which won the prize, is my friend.
explanation: A RESTRICTIVE CLAUSE (no commas) identifies which student. A non-restrictive clause (with commas) would add extra information. WHO is correct for people; WHICH is for things.

questionText: Complete: 'He is one of those students who ___ regularly.'
options: A) studies
B) study
C) is studying
D) has studied
explanation: In 'one of those students who STUDY,' the relative clause modifies STUDENTS (plural), so the verb is plural: STUDY.

questionText: Which sentence uses the passive voice correctly?
options: A) The report was written by she.
B) The report was written by her.
C) The report has wrote by her.
D) The report is wrote by her.
explanation: In passive sentences, the agent (doer) follows BY and uses the OBJECT pronoun form: BY HER, not BY SHE.

questionText: Choose the correctly formed complex sentence:
options: A) Although she was tired but she continued.
B) Although she was tired, she continued.
C) Although she was tired, yet she continued.
D) She was tired although but she continued.
explanation: ALTHOUGH is a subordinating conjunction that already implies contrast — do not add BUT or YET after it. Correct: Although..., [main clause].

questionText: Identify the dangling modifier in the options:
options: A) Running to catch the bus, the girl dropped her bag.
B) Running to catch the bus, the bag was dropped.
C) The girl, running to catch the bus, dropped her bag.
D) The bag was dropped by the girl running to catch the bus.
explanation: In option B, the participial phrase RUNNING TO CATCH THE BUS has no clear subject — the bag cannot run. This is a DANGLING MODIFIER.

questionText: Complete the sentence: 'The data ___ collected over five years.'
options: A) was
B) were
C) is
D) Both A and B depending on context
explanation: DATA is the plural of DATUM. Formally, data WERE is correct. However, in modern usage DATA IS/WAS is widely accepted. Both depend on context and style guide.

questionText: Which is the correctly formed reported speech for: 'She said, I will come tomorrow.'
options: A) She said that she will come tomorrow.
B) She said that she would come the next day.
C) She said that she would come tomorrow.
D) She told that she would come the next day.
explanation: In reported speech, WILL changes to WOULD, and time expressions shift: TOMORROW becomes THE NEXT DAY. SAID is correct here (not TOLD, which requires an object).

questionText: Which sentence correctly uses an em-dash?
options: A) She had one goal—to win the championship.
B) She had one goal - to win the championship.
C) She had one goal; to win the championship.
D) She had one goal, to win the championship.
explanation: An EM-DASH (—) is used for emphasis before a restatement or elaboration. It is longer than a hyphen and has no spaces around it in standard usage.

questionText: Choose the correct sentence with an absolute phrase:
options: A) Her work complete, she left the office.
B) Her work was complete, she left the office.
C) Her work being complete and she left the office.
D) Complete her work, she left the office.
explanation: An ABSOLUTE PHRASE modifies the entire main clause and consists of a noun + participial: HER WORK COMPLETE. It is separated from the main clause by a comma.

questionText: Complete: 'No sooner ___ he arrived ___ it started raining.'
options: A) did / when
B) had / than
C) has / when
D) did / than
explanation: NO SOONER + past perfect → THAN: No sooner HAD he arrived THAN it started raining. This is an inverted structure for emphasis.

questionText: Which sentence avoids a comma splice?
options: A) She was tired, she went to bed.
B) She was tired; she went to bed.
C) She was tired, went to bed.
D) She was tired and went to bed.
explanation: A COMMA SPLICE joins two independent clauses with only a comma. Correct options: use a semicolon (B), a coordinating conjunction (D), or a full stop. Option C is incomplete.

questionText: Which sentence uses WHOM correctly?
options: A) Whom shall I say is calling?
B) Who did you speak to?
C) To whom did you address the letter?
D) Who did she give the award to?
explanation: WHOM is used as an object pronoun. TO WHOM is correct because whom is the object of the preposition TO. Option A should use WHO (subject of is calling).

questionText: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence:
options: A) Its a beautiful day, isnt it?
B) It's a beautiful day, isn't it?
C) Its a beautiful day isn't it?
D) It's a beautiful day isn't it?
explanation: IT'S (with apostrophe) is the contraction of IT IS. ISN'T (with apostrophe) is the contraction of IS NOT. Commas are used before tag questions.

questionText: Complete: '___ you help me with this, I will finish on time.'
options: A) Although
B) Unless
C) However
D) Therefore
explanation: UNLESS means if not: UNLESS you help me = IF you do NOT help me. The sentence means: help is required to finish on time.

questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the future perfect tense?
options: A) By tomorrow, I finish the report.
B) By tomorrow, I will finish the report.
C) By tomorrow, I will have finished the report.
D) By tomorrow, I had finished the report.
explanation: FUTURE PERFECT (will have + past participle) describes an action that will be completed before a specific future time: will have finished by tomorrow.

questionText: Identify the sentence with a misplaced modifier:
options: A) She almost drove her kids to school every day.
B) She drove her kids to school every day.
C) She drove almost every day to school.
D) Almost every day, she drove her kids to school.
explanation: ALMOST should be placed before EVERY DAY, not before DROVE — option A implies she nearly drove but did not. Correct: She drove her kids to school almost every day.

questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon?
options: A) She loves poetry; and novels.
B) She loves poetry; she reads every night.
C) She loves; poetry and novels.
D) She loves poetry, and she; reads every night.
explanation: A SEMICOLON joins two independent clauses without a conjunction. Option B correctly connects two complete sentences.

questionText: Complete the sentence: 'I wish I ___ fluent in three languages.'
options: A) am
B) was
C) were
D) will be
explanation: After WISH, the subjunctive form WERE is used for present/unreal situations. I wish I WERE rich (but I am not).

questionText: Which sentence demonstrates correct use of an appositive?
options: A) My sister, a doctor, she works in Delhi.
B) My sister a doctor works in Delhi.
C) My sister, a doctor, works in Delhi.
D) My sister who is a doctor, works in Delhi.
explanation: An APPOSITIVE is a noun phrase placed beside another noun to identify or describe it, set off by commas: My sister, A DOCTOR, works in Delhi.

questionText: Choose the correctly formed sentence using inversion:
options: A) Rarely I have seen such courage.
B) Rarely have I seen such courage.
C) Rarely I have seen courage such.
D) Rarely I seen have such courage.
explanation: When a negative or restrictive adverb (RARELY, NEVER, SELDOM) starts a sentence, the subject and auxiliary invert: RARELY HAVE I SEEN.

questionText: Complete: 'The principal, along with all the teachers, ___ the ceremony.'
options: A) attend
B) attending
C) attends
D) attend to
explanation: The subject is THE PRINCIPAL (singular). ALONG WITH is a prepositional phrase — it does not change the subject. So the verb is ATTENDS (singular).

questionText: Which sentence is correctly structured in the third conditional?
options: A) If I knew, I would have told you.
B) If I had known, I would have told you.
C) If I had known, I would tell you.
D) If I have known, I will tell you.
explanation: THIRD CONDITIONAL: If + past perfect → would have + past participle. If I HAD KNOWN, I WOULD HAVE TOLD you.

questionText: Identify the sentence that avoids a run-on:
options: A) It was raining we could not go.
B) It was raining so we could not go.
C) It was raining, we could not go.
D) It was raining but we could not go either.
explanation: Option B uses SO (coordinating conjunction) to properly connect two independent clauses, avoiding a run-on. Option C is a comma splice; option A has no connector.

questionText: Choose the sentence with correct subject-verb agreement:
options: A) Either the boys or the girl are responsible.
B) Either the boys or the girl is responsible.
C) Either the boy or the girls is responsible.
D) Either the boys or the girls is responsible.
explanation: With EITHER...OR, the verb agrees with the NEAREST subject: THE GIRL (singular), so the verb is IS.

questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a colon?
options: A) She needs: rest, water, and food.
B) She needs rest: water and food.
C) She needs three things: rest, water, and food.
D) She: needs rest, water, and food.
explanation: A COLON is used after a complete clause to introduce a list or explanation. Option C is correct: She needs three things: [list].

questionText: Complete: 'By the time she arrived, the meeting ___.'
options: A) ended
B) had ended
C) has ended
D) ends
explanation: The PAST PERFECT (had ended) is used for an action that was completed before another past action. By the time she arrived = before she arrived, the meeting had ended.

questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a reflexive pronoun?
options: A) He hurt him during the game.
B) He hurt himself during the game.
C) He hurt themselves during the game.
D) He hurts hisself during the game.
explanation: HIMSELF is the correct reflexive pronoun for HE — when the subject and object of the verb refer to the same person. HISSELF is not a standard word.

questionText: Choose the sentence with correct article usage:
options: A) She is a honest woman.
B) She is an honest woman.
C) She is the honest woman.
D) She is honest a woman.
explanation: AN is used before words beginning with a vowel SOUND. HONEST begins with a silent H — the first sound is the vowel /o/ — so AN HONEST is correct.

questionText: Which sentence is correctly formed using ellipsis?
options: A) She can speak French and I can French too.
B) She can speak French and I can too.
C) She can speak French and I too can speak.
D) She can speak French and I too can.
explanation: ELLIPSIS means omitting repeated words: I CAN (speak French) TOO. Option B correctly omits SPEAK FRENCH to avoid repetition.

questionText: Complete: 'It is essential that every citizen ___ their rights.'
options: A) knows
B) know
C) is knowing
D) has known
explanation: After expressions like IT IS ESSENTIAL/IMPORTANT THAT, the SUBJUNCTIVE (base form of verb) is used: that every citizen KNOW (not knows).

questionText: Which sentence correctly uses the present perfect continuous?
options: A) She has been study for hours.
B) She has been studying for hours.
C) She had been studying for hours.
D) She have been studying for hours.
explanation: PRESENT PERFECT CONTINUOUS: HAS/HAVE + BEEN + verb-ING. SHE HAS BEEN STUDYING shows an action that started in the past and continues now.

questionText: Choose the correctly formed negative question:
options: A) Didn't she not arrive on time?
B) Did she not arrive on time?
C) Did not she arrive on time?
D) Did she arrive not on time?
explanation: Negative questions use DID + subject + NOT + base verb: DID SHE NOT ARRIVE, or the contracted: Didn't she arrive on time?

questionText: Identify the correctly formed emphatic sentence:
options: A) She do love poetry.
B) She does love poetry.
C) She does loves poetry.
D) She loves poetry does.
explanation: The auxiliary DO/DOES is used for emphasis in affirmative sentences: She DOES love poetry. After DOES, the base form (love) is used.

questionText: Complete: 'The more you practice, ___ you become.'
options: A) the more better
B) the better
C) more better
D) the most good
explanation: THE MORE...THE BETTER is the standard double comparative structure. THE + comparative, THE + comparative.

questionText: Which sentence correctly uses a gerund as a subject?
options: A) To swim in cold water is refreshing.
B) Swimming in cold water is refreshing.
C) Swim in cold water is refreshing.
D) Both A and B are correct
explanation: Both SWIMMING (gerund) and TO SWIM (infinitive) can function as subjects of a sentence. Both option A and B are grammatically correct.

questionText: Choose the correct formation: 'She asked me ___.'
options: A) what time was it
B) what time it was
C) what is the time
D) the time that it was
explanation: In INDIRECT QUESTIONS, the word order changes to statement order (subject before verb): she asked me WHAT TIME IT WAS, not WHAT TIME WAS IT.

questionText: Which sentence uses LEST correctly?
options: A) Be careful lest you fall.
B) Be careful lest you will fall.
C) Be careful lest that you fall.
D) Be careful so lest you fall.
explanation: LEST means for fear that. It is followed by the subjunctive (base form without to): LEST YOU FALL. Do not use WILL or WOULD after LEST.

questionText: Complete: 'No sooner had the bell rung ___ the students rushed out.'
options: A) when
B) then
C) than
D) after
explanation: NO SOONER is paired with THAN — not WHEN or THEN: No sooner had the bell rung THAN the students rushed out.

questionText: Which sentence is correctly written using a participial phrase?
options: A) Exhausted by the heat, the hikers rested.
B) Exhausted by the heat, resting was done by the hikers.
C) The hikers, exhausted the heat, rested.
D) Rested, exhausted by the heat, the hikers.
explanation: A PARTICIPIAL PHRASE (EXHAUSTED BY THE HEAT) must be placed directly before or after the noun it modifies — here, THE HIKERS. Option A correctly places it at the start.

questionText: Choose the sentence that correctly uses AS WELL AS:
options: A) He as well as his friends are going.
B) He as well as his friends is going.
C) He as well as his friends were going.
D) He as well as his friends going.
subTopic: subject-verb agreement with as well as
explanation: AS WELL AS is a prepositional phrase, not a conjunction. The subject remains HE (singular), so the verb is IS.

questionText: Which sentence correctly uses SCARCELY in an inverted construction?
options: A) Scarcely I had sat down when the phone rang.
B) Scarcely had I sat down when the phone rang.
C) Scarcely had I sat down than the phone rang.
D) I had scarcely sat down when rang the phone.
explanation: SCARCELY triggers inversion of subject and auxiliary: SCARCELY HAD I... It is followed by WHEN (not THAN), unlike NO SOONER.

questionText: Complete: 'I would rather you ___ here quietly.'
options: A) stay
B) stayed
C) will stay
D) have stayed
explanation: WOULD RATHER + second subject takes the PAST TENSE (not the base form): I would rather you STAYED. This expresses preference about someone else actions.

questionText: Which sentence uses HAVING + past participle correctly?
options: A) Having finished the report, she submitted it.
B) Having finished the report, it was submitted.
C) Having finish the report, she submitted it.
D) She having finished submitted the report.
explanation: HAVING + past participle forms a perfect participial phrase showing that one action was completed before another: HAVING FINISHED, she submitted (then). The subject must match the main clause.

questionText: Identify the sentence with correct use of HARDLY:
options: A) Hardly the children arrived when it began to snow.
B) Hardly had the children arrived when it began to snow.
C) Hardly had the children arrived than it began to snow.
D) The children had hardly arrived when begun to snow it.
explanation: HARDLY triggers subject-auxiliary inversion and is followed by WHEN: HARDLY HAD the children arrived WHEN it began to snow.
